strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating ML-engineering agents that can exploit community knowledge rather than operating in a closed environment.

MLE-Live incorporates thousands of discussions and public kernels with timestamps and metadata, and the restriction to artifacts published before competition deadlines is a sensible safeguard against direct post-hoc leakage.

The evaluation spans 20 competitions and several modalities under a shared LLM, hardware budget, and execution budget. CoMind reports substantial improvements over AIDE variants, including a win rate of 66.8% and nine medal-level results.
The four ongoing Kaggle competitions provide a useful reality check based on official leaderboard submissions rather than only locally reconstructed graders.
The presentation is generally clear, with an intuitive workflow diagram, relevant baseline extensions, a resource-access ablation, and an explicit broader-impact discussion.
weaknesses: The method is substantially underspecified. The paper does not provide prompts, idea-selection criteria, pool sizes, iteration schedules, number and synchronization of parallel agents, resource-summarization procedures, or other details needed to reproduce CoMind. No code or benchmark release is identified.

The central attribution to community-driven exploration is not convincingly isolated. The only ablation removes all public resources; there are no ablations of the idea pool, report pool, iterative synthesis, parallel-agent exchange, discussion versus kernel access, or the claimed context-management mechanism.

Baseline access to community information is not clearly matched to CoMind. AIDE+Code receives only one highest-voted kernel per draft, while AIDE+RAG first considers ten highly voted titles. CoMind appears to use a much richer curated pool and its own summaries, so the results may reflect unequal information access rather than the proposed agent design.

Results appear to come from one stochastic run per competition. The paper reports no repeated trials, uncertainty intervals, significance tests, or per-task scores, making the sizable aggregate claims difficult to assess. Several task categories contain only one example.

The benchmark may reward retrieval or adaptation of competition-specific public solutions rather than general ML-engineering ability. Timestamp filtering alone does not address benchmark contamination in the backend LLM, near-copying of public kernels, or the possibility that public artifacts encode solutions closely aligned with the reconstructed test set.

Comparisons to humans are potentially misleading. Kaggle leaderboard participants operate under heterogeneous time, compute, submission, and collaboration conditions, whereas the agent receives a fixed five-hour run. Consequently, statements such as outperforming 79.2% of humans are not controlled head-to-head comparisons.

The live evaluation covers only four competitions and does not report submission counts, submission-selection policy, evaluation dates, private-leaderboard results, run variance, or safeguards against public-leaderboard overfitting. The standings are transient and may not represent final performance.

The novelty evaluation lacks essential protocol details: sample size, expert qualifications, rubric, blinding, annotator agreement, and statistical analysis. Average ranks alone do not substantiate the claim of genuinely novel methods.

Code length is treated as evidence of sophistication and deeper reasoning, but longer code can instead indicate redundancy or poor abstraction. No code-quality, correctness, efficiency, or maintainability assessment supports this interpretation.

Important inconsistencies and omissions remain: 22 competitions are collected but only 20 are evaluated without explanation; the multi-agent collaboration claim is not separately evaluated; and the paper does not analyze cost, token use, or compute efficiency despite comparing agents with materially different workflows.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and practically important question: whether ML-engineering agents can benefit from community discussions and public code. The manuscript is readable, and the high-level MLE-Live/CoMind workflow is communicated clearly. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/f3cd111d1e1145b580e5eb0a8c73bd48/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The evaluation covers 20 historical competitions from several task categories and four ongoing competitions, all under a stated five-hour hardware budget and the same o4-mini backend.

CoMind reports a meaningful aggregate improvement over AIDE: 0.668 versus 0.512 average win rate, alongside higher valid-submission and medal rates. The direct submissions to ongoing Kaggle leaderboards provide useful evidence beyond purely local grading.
The resource-removal ablation suggests that public discussions and kernels materially improve performance, reducing average win rate from 0.668 to 0.545 when removed.
weaknesses: The central causal claim is not adequately established. The only ablation removes all public resources; it does not isolate idea selection, the idea/report pools, iterative synthesis, parallel agents, or inter-agent sharing. Consequently, the results show that access to task-specific public solutions helps, but not that CoMind's proposed community mechanism is responsible for the gain.

The comparison may be substantially confounded by unequal access and processing of community information. AIDE+Code receives one top-voted kernel per draft and AIDE+RAG retrieves from ten titles, whereas CoMind appears able to build pools from thousands of artifacts. Resource counts, token budgets, numbers of model calls, parallel instances, iterations, and summarization procedures are not reported or matched.

The benchmark can expose agents to near-complete public kernels for the exact target competitions. Although these were posted before competition deadlines, the paper does not quantify copying, contamination, or overlap with evaluated solutions. Calling the resulting performance research innovation or deeper reasoning is therefore too strong.

The empirical reporting is insufficiently rigorous for stochastic LLM agents: apparently only one run is performed per task, with no repeated trials, confidence intervals, significance tests, or sensitivity analysis. Several category-level conclusions rest on only one task.

Reproducibility is poor. The paper provides no release commitment or sufficiently detailed specification of prompts, task identities, data reconstruction, artifact filtering, timestamps, pool construction, stopping rules, agent count, generated code, or grading scripts. It also says 22 competitions were collected but reports evaluation on only 20 without explaining the exclusion.

The novelty evaluation is not credible as presented. It omits the number and qualifications of evaluators, number of solutions, rubric, blinding, assignment protocol, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty. The assertion that external ideas were excluded is also not operationalized.

Code length is treated as evidence of complexity, richer optimization, and deeper reasoning, but character count is not a valid quality measure and may merely capture verbosity or redundant code. No qualitative or functional complexity analysis supports this interpretation.

There are reporting inconsistencies: Figure 3 appears to give CoMind an Any Medal rate of 0.400, while Table 3 reports 0.45 and the text claims nine medals out of 20. The abstract's 79.2% ongoing-competition figure also does not transparently follow from Table 4's displayed win rates, whose simple average is approximately 79.4%.

The online evaluation uses only four mutable leaderboards, including competitions with as few as 47–48 participants, and does not clarify public versus private leaderboard status, submission selection, or checkpoint date. These results are encouraging but not robust evidence of broad real-world superiority.

Deploying automated agents in active competitions raises compliance, licensing, attribution, and fairness concerns, especially when public kernels are reused. The broader-impact section does not address competition rules, consent, plagiarism safeguards, or licenses of the collected artifacts.

Overall, the benchmark direction is promising and the raw results are encouraging, but the limited novelty, opaque and potentially unfair comparison, weak causal ablations, lack of statistical validation, and poor reproducibility leave the main claims insufficiently supported for a top-tier acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored question: evaluating ML-engineering agents that use community discussions and public code rather than operating in isolation.
MLE-Live is a useful benchmark direction, assembling 2,687 discussions and 4,270 kernels from 22 competitions with timestamps and quality metadata.

The evaluation is broad and practically relevant: 20 historical competitions across seven task categories plus four live Kaggle competitions. CoMind achieves a 0.668 average historical win rate, valid submissions on all 20 tasks, and outperforms AIDE in all four live competitions.

The comparison uses the same backend model, hardware limits, and overall time budget. The AIDE+Code and AIDE+RAG variants help demonstrate that naive access to community resources alone does not explain CoMind's full advantage.

The paper is clearly organized, includes concrete resource constraints, and discusses limitations and broader impacts. weaknesses: The evidence does not isolate the main architectural claims. The only ablation removes all public resources; there are no ablations of the idea pool, report pool, selection and synthesis stages, parallel drafts, iterative reporting, or multi-agent sharing. It is therefore unclear which proposed components cause the gain.

The paper apparently reports one run per agent and competition, without variance, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. LLM-agent outcomes can be highly stochastic, making differences such as CoMind's 0.668 versus roughly 0.51 for AIDE difficult to assess reliably.

Reproducibility is insufficient: the manuscript provides no code or benchmark release link and omits prompts, sampling settings, numbers of parallel agents and iterations, idea-ranking details, communication schedules, token/API costs, and several implementation choices.

Historical evaluation may be affected by contamination because the 2025 backend model could have encountered these past Kaggle competitions and their solutions during training. Timestamping retrieved resources prevents post-deadline retrieval leakage but does not address model pretraining contamination. The four live tasks partly mitigate this concern but form a small, non-random sample.

The benchmark construction is underspecified. It is unclear why 20 of the 22 collected competitions are evaluated, how reconstructed train-test splits relate to original Kaggle leaderboards, and whether human win-rate and medal thresholds remain comparable when test sets or graders are reconstructed.

Baseline coverage is narrow for a state-of-the-art claim: evaluation centers on AIDE and author-created AIDE variants, without empirical comparisons to several related MLE/AutoML agents discussed in the paper.

The novelty evaluation lacks essential protocol details, including the number and expertise of evaluators, number of solutions assessed, blinding, rubric, inter-rater agreement, and uncertainty. Average ranks alone do not convincingly establish methodological novelty.

Code length is not a valid proxy for complexity, sophistication, or deeper reasoning; longer generated programs may instead reflect verbosity or duplication. Claims based on this metric should be removed or supported by substantive code-quality analysis.

Given the strong empirical signal but substantial attribution, statistical, contamination, and reproducibility gaps, the paper is promising yet marginally below the acceptance threshold in its current form.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored question: evaluating ML-engineering agents that exploit community knowledge rather than operating in a closed, isolated environment.
MLE-Live is potentially a valuable benchmark resource, covering 75 diverse Kaggle competitions and a substantial collection of 15,733 kernels and 12,951 discussions with temporal metadata.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. In addition to the retrospective benchmark, the authors evaluate CoMind on eight ongoing competitions using genuine Kaggle submissions, providing useful evidence beyond static benchmark scores.

The controlled 20-task study uses the same backend model for all methods and compares against strengthened AIDE variants with code and retrieval access. Its results provide some evidence that community resources and sustained exploration improve performance.

The system is reasonably well motivated and decomposes the workflow into understandable roles. Compute limits, token usage, monetary cost, prompts, and an illustrative failure analysis are also reported.
weaknesses: The headline state-of-the-art comparison is not controlled. Table 1 combines leaderboard results produced with different language models, scaffolds, compute budgets, and evaluation dates. CoMind's 36.00% medal rate is only slightly above Neo's 34.22%, corresponding to roughly one or two tasks, yet no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance test support the claim that it significantly outperforms prior systems.

The retrospective protocol has unresolved contamination and temporal-validity risks. MLE-Bench can reconstruct test sets from original public training data, while the retrieved notebooks were developed using the original competition data and feedback. Restricting access to external datasets does not fully establish that notebook code, preprocessing decisions, or embedded artifacts cannot exploit information related to reconstructed examples. Moreover, giving an agent a curated collection of all pre-deadline artifacts at once does not reproduce the information available to a human at any particular point in the competition.

The ablation study does not cleanly isolate the claimed innovations. CoMind is compared with AIDE variants while also differing in orchestration, parallelism, memory, number of coding trajectories, and possibly effective compute. Component ablations for the Analyzer, Idea Proposer, persistent memory, dependency graph, parallel coding, and evaluator are missing. CoMind without resources only establishes a joint resource-access effect, not the value of the proposed multi-agent design.

Reproducibility is insufficient for a benchmark/system contribution. The manuscript provides no code or dataset release location, only example prompts, and leaves important procedures vague, including artifact curation, strategic sampling, dependency-graph construction and use, split generation across task types, and final solution selection. Full per-task results for the 75-task experiment are also absent.

The live evaluation is promising but difficult to interpret rigorously. The eight competitions appear opportunistically selected, leaderboard snapshots and submission dates are not reported, rankings in ongoing competitions are provisional, and there is no discussion of selection criteria, submission limits, repeated attempts, or compliance and disclosure considerations. Comparisons to the best public notebook also do not necessarily measure performance against the strongest competitors.

The novelty of CoMind itself is moderate: specialized-agent orchestration, parallel candidate generation, retrieval of public solutions, memory, and iterative evaluation are familiar ingredients. The paper describes the community as interactive, but experimentally it is largely a static retrieval corpus augmented with the system's own outputs rather than a community of independent agents or humans.

Several analyses are weakly connected to solution quality. In particular, longer and more complex code is presented positively even though it can indicate unnecessary complexity, and CoMind often has lower Pylint scores. The paper does not demonstrate that this added complexity causally contributes to performance.

The limitations section is too narrow and does not address the main threats involving retrospective leakage, unequal baseline resources, benchmark maintenance, live-evaluation ethics, or the high compute and token requirements.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and important problem: evaluating ML-engineering agents that can exploit public community knowledge rather than operating in isolation.
MLE-Live aggregates a substantial collection of 15,733 kernels and 12,951 discussions from 75 diverse Kaggle competitions, with an explicit attempt to filter artifacts by publication time.

The empirical scope is unusually broad. It includes all 75 MLE-Bench competitions, a controlled 20-task study, and submissions to eight ongoing competitions; the reported leaderboard performance is promising.
The appendix provides useful implementation information, including agent prompts, hardware and time limits, token costs, resource statistics, and an extended qualitative case study.
weaknesses: The headline MLE-Bench comparison is not controlled. CoMind receives public competition kernels and discussions, whereas the leaderboard baselines generally did not receive equivalent information and may use different models, compute budgets, or execution protocols. Consequently, the 36.00% versus 34.22% result does not isolate an algorithmic advantage of CoMind.

The paper calls the improvement over prior work significant without reporting repeated runs, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or even task-level outcomes. The 1.78-point advantage over Neo corresponds to roughly one or two competitions and could readily reflect stochastic variation.

The ablation study does not establish which proposed components matter. There are no controlled ablations of the Analyzer, Idea Proposer, persistent memory, dependency graph, parallel coding, or iterative publication mechanism. Comparisons with AIDE variants also lack matched LLM-token, agent-call, and parallel-compute budgets.

The retrospective protocol raises contamination and post-hoc-selection concerns. CoMind is given top-voted solutions collected up to each competition deadline, potentially including mature near-winning pipelines. This is not equivalent to the information available to participants throughout a competition, and the paper does not evaluate temporally synchronized snapshots. Restricting external datasets does not fully resolve leakage risks when MLE-Bench test sets are reconstructed from formerly public training data.

The live evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous for the claims made. The eight competitions appear selectively chosen, the selection criterion is not given, ranks are provisional public-leaderboard ranks rather than final private-leaderboard results, and the number of submissions or amount of leaderboard feedback is unspecified. Comparison against the best public kernel is also not comparison against the best human competitor.

The methodological novelty is limited. The architecture mainly combines conventional role-based prompting, retrieval of public solutions, parallel coding agents, and iterative evaluation. The claimed dependency graph is not operationally specified or experimentally validated, and the simulated community is closer to a static artifact repository plus internal memory than genuine community interaction.

Important implementation details are inconsistent or underspecified. For example, the Analyzer's main-text description includes multidimensional scoring, while its provided prompt primarily performs pipeline distillation; resource-sampling and graph-prioritization algorithms are not defined precisely.

The LLM-generated Evaluator is a potential source of invalid evaluation. A generic 90/10 split can be inappropriate for grouped, temporal, multilabel, or distribution-shifted competitions, yet no systematic audit of split correctness, metric fidelity, or correlation with leaderboard performance is reported.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the extensive prompt appendix: there is no clear code or MLE-Live release, no complete per-task results, limited random-seed information, and reliance on a proprietary dated model. Only CoMind's token cost is reported, preventing efficiency-normalized comparison.

The claim that longer and more complex code is evidence of richer or better solutions is poorly motivated; code length and higher complexity may instead indicate unnecessary complexity or reduced maintainability.

The paper does not discuss compliance with Kaggle rules, disclosure of automated participation, effects on ongoing competitors, or other competition-integrity concerns arising from deploying autonomous multi-agent systems in live contests.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: evaluating ML-engineering agents that can exploit community knowledge rather than operating in a fully isolated environment.
MLE-Live is a potentially valuable benchmark extension, collecting 15,733 kernels and 12,951 discussions across all 75 MLE-Bench competitions while attempting to enforce temporal cutoffs.

The empirical scope is unusually broad, combining retrospective evaluation on 75 competitions, controlled comparisons on 20 MLE-Bench-Lite tasks, and deployment in eight ongoing competitions spanning several modalities.
The live results are impressive: CoMind reportedly outperforms 92.6% of competitors on average and reaches the top 5% in three competitions, providing evidence beyond static benchmark performance.

The same-backend comparison against AIDE, AIDE+Code, and AIDE+RAG supports the conclusion that richer community-aware exploration can improve average win rate. The prompts, compute limits, token usage, cost, and an extensive case study also provide useful implementation detail.
weaknesses: The central retrospective evaluation has an unresolved contamination risk. MLE-Bench test sets can be reconstructed from original public training data, while public kernels, checkpoints, predictions, and submission artifacts may have used those examples and labels. The paper says public datasets are restricted, but other sections and prompts explicitly permit referenced models, kernel outputs, and external submissions. The exact artifact-sanitization policy is therefore unclear, and restricting datasets alone does not rule out leakage.

The claimed state-of-the-art improvement is not statistically substantiated. CoMind's 36.00% medal rate is only 1.78 percentage points above Neo, corresponding to roughly one competition, yet no repeated runs, confidence intervals, paired task-level results, or significance tests are reported. The statement that the method “significantly” outperforms prior agents is unsupported.

The leaderboard comparison does not adequately control backend models, inference budgets, hardware, number of attempts, or access to community resources. Numbers copied from the MLE-Bench leaderboard are consequently not a clean controlled comparison of agent architectures.

The 20-task ablation is small and apparently based on one run per method. Several differences amount to only one competition, no uncertainty is shown, and CoMind loses to retrieval baselines in some categories. Moreover, there are no component ablations for the Coordinator, Analyzer, Idea Proposer, persistent memory, parallel coding, or iterative publication mechanism, so the gains cannot be attributed to the proposed architecture.

The framing of a simulated “community” is stronger than the implemented interaction. CoMind primarily consumes a fixed set of top-voted historical artifacts and adds its own outputs to an internal pool; it does not model independent community members, responses, evolving external contributions, or reciprocal communication. This is closer to artifact retrieval plus iterative multi-agent search than a demonstrated community-driven ecosystem.

The eight live competitions may provide valuable ecological evidence, but their selection criteria, evaluation dates, submission counts, and public-versus-private leaderboard status are insufficiently documented. Without a preregistered or exhaustive selection protocol, selection bias and transient public-leaderboard overfitting cannot be excluded.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the extensive prompt appendix: the paper provides no clear release statement or repository for MLE-Live, CoMind, per-task outputs, artifact manifests, dependency graph construction, or evaluation scripts. The dataset collection, deduplication, missing-resource handling, licensing, and exact temporal verification procedures are also underspecified.

The paper lacks a meaningful ethics discussion. Automated participation in ongoing competitions can affect human rankings and prize-bearing contests, while scraping and redistributing community code, discussions, datasets, and models raises attribution, licensing, privacy, and platform-policy questions.

Some analytical evidence is weakly motivated: longer code and higher complexity are treated as positive indicators even though they do not establish solution quality and may instead reduce maintainability. The manuscript also contains numerous grammatical and presentation issues that should be corrected.
